title: Four, or three?
prompt:
You're checking a lab summary before it goes out. Normal potassium is
about 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L, and the script counts the patients over 5.5:

```r
nrow(labs[labs$k > 5.5, ])
```

It says `4`. Open the **Data** panel and count for yourself — you'll find
three.

Before you trust any result, look at how R sees the data. Run this:

```r
str(labs)
```

Why does the script count four?
hint:
Look at the type `str()` gives for `k`. Then find which patient the script
counted that you didn't.

options.text: `k` is stored as text, so R compares it alphabetically — and "hemolysed" comes out as higher than 5.5
options.feedback:
Right. `str()` says `k` is `chr`: one result reads "hemolysed", so the
whole column became text. And when R compares text with a number, it
compares them as text — character by character, the way a dictionary
orders words. Letters sort after digits, so "hemolysed" counts as
higher than 5.5. Worse: a potassium of 10.2 would count as *lower*,
because "1" comes before "5".

Nothing warned you. In the Data panel, `5.6` looks like a number either
way. What caught it was counting by hand — a *sanity check* — and then
`str()` to see why.

options.text: The missing value added a phantom row, like in module 8
options.feedback:
That was a good guess for module 8, but there's no `NA` in `k`. The
fourth patient the script counted is 103 — the hemolysed sample.
Running `str(labs)` shows why.

options.text: One patient is listed twice
options.feedback:
All eight patients appear once. The extra one counted is patient 103,
whose result is "hemolysed". Run `str(labs)` and look at `k`'s type.

options.text: Values of exactly 5.5 are being counted
options.feedback:
Nobody has a potassium of exactly 5.5. The extra patient is 103, the
hemolysed sample. Look at `k`'s type in `str(labs)`.

title: The same answer, a second way
prompt:
A good sanity check is to get the same answer by a different route. Convert
`k` to numbers, and count the TRUEs.

Fill in the blank so the hemolysed result doesn't spoil the count.
hint:
`as.numeric()` will turn "hemolysed" into `NA`. You've told `mean()` and
`sum()` what to do about missing values before.

solution.why:
Three — the same as your count. Two different methods agreeing is what
lets you trust the answer.

You'll also see *NAs introduced by coercion*: that's "hemolysed" turning
into `NA`, and `na.rm = TRUE` then leaving it out. Here that's what you
want — but it's a decision, and the next exercise is about not losing
track of it.

checks.on_fail: Not 3 yet. Check that the missing value is being left out of the count.

misconceptions.feedback:
`NA` — the hemolysed result became a missing value, and it's spoiling
the whole count. Tell `sum()` to leave missing values out.
Inside a call, give an argument its value with `=`, not `<-`.

title: Keeping the note
prompt:
A *hemolysed* sample is one where red blood cells broke open after the
blood was drawn. They release potassium, so the result reads falsely high,
and the test needs repeating.

To fix `k` for good, the quickest option is:

```r
labs$k <- as.numeric(labs$k)
```

Another is:

```r
labs$k_num <- as.numeric(labs$k)
```

Why is the second safer?
hint: After each line, what has happened to the word "hemolysed"?

options.text: The original `k` keeps "hemolysed", which tells you that sample needs redrawing
options.feedback:
Right. Storing into `labs$k` replaces it, silently, and "hemolysed"
becomes `NA` for good. But `NA` could mean anything: never drawn, lost,
hemolysed. Clinically those aren't the same — a hemolysed sample means
the patient needs another draw, and their real potassium is still
unknown. Once the word is gone, nobody reading the data later can
tell.

Putting the numbers in a new column keeps both: numbers you can
calculate with, and the original telling you *why* one is missing.

options.text: Neither is safer — they give the same numbers
options.feedback:
The numbers are the same, but the first line also throws something
away: the word "hemolysed", which tells you why that result is missing.

options.text: The first is better — fewer columns is tidier
options.feedback:
Tidier, but it overwrites `k`, and "hemolysed" becomes `NA` for good.
The reason the value is missing is information worth keeping.

title: An average that can't be right
prompt:
The script also reports the average creatinine, in mg/dL:

```r
mean(labs$creat)
```

```
[1] 11.8625
```

A normal adult creatinine is roughly 0.6 to 1.3 mg/dL. There was no error
and no warning. Before you put that in a report, what's your first move?

options.text: Look at the spread of the values, with `summary(labs$creat)`
options.feedback:
Right. A typical creatinine is around 1 mg/dL. An average near 12
across a ward of patients isn't plausible — something in there is
wildly off. `summary()` shows the whole spread in one line, so you can
see what it is.

Nothing in R can tell you 11.86 is wrong. It ran perfectly. Only
someone who knows what a creatinine should be can see it — the same
lesson as MAP in module 2.

options.text: Round it to 11.9 for the report
options.feedback:
Rounding a wrong number makes a tidier wrong number. A typical
creatinine is around 1 mg/dL — an average near 12 should stop you.

options.text: Add `na.rm = TRUE`
options.feedback:
There's no missing value here — the mean came back as a number, not
`NA`. The problem is that number: about twelve times a normal
creatinine.

options.text: Nothing — there's no error or warning, so it's fine
options.feedback:
That's exactly the trap in this module. R ran without complaint and
still gave an answer no clinician would believe.

title: Reading the spread
prompt:
`summary(labs$creat)` gives:

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
  0.000   0.975   1.150  11.863   1.325  88.000
```

Which values look wrong, and why?
hint:
Look at the two ends — the minimum and the maximum. And compare the mean
with the median. One more thing that helps: creatinine is sometimes
reported in µmol/L instead of mg/dL, and 1 mg/dL is 88.4 µmol/L.

options.text: The 0, which can't be a real creatinine, and the 88, which looks like a different unit
options.feedback:
Right — two different problems. A creatinine of 0 isn't possible; it's
almost certainly a missing result someone typed as zero, like the
weight in module 6. And 88 is about what a normal creatinine looks like
in µmol/L. Divide by 88.4 and it's 1.0 mg/dL — one result reported in
the wrong unit.

Notice the median: 1.15, perfectly normal, while the mean is 11.86.
When the mean and median are far apart, a few values are pulling the
mean, and `summary()` shows you both side by side.

options.text: Only the 88
options.feedback:
The 88 is one — it's probably in µmol/L, not mg/dL. But look at the
minimum too: a creatinine of 0 isn't possible.

options.text: None — the median of 1.15 is normal
options.feedback:
The median is normal, which is exactly the clue. The mean is ten times
higher, so something is pulling it. Look at the minimum and maximum.

title: Fixing one value, and nothing else
prompt:
You decide the 0 should be a missing value. Which line does that, and
changes nothing else?
hint: Read each one inside out. Which ones change more than the single 0?

options.text: `labs$creat[labs$creat == 0] <- NA`
options.feedback:
Right. Read it inside out: `labs$creat == 0` asks which values are
zero; the square brackets pick out just those; and `<- NA` stores a
missing value there. Every other value, and every other column, stays
as it was. You'll see this pattern often in generated code.

options.text: `labs <- filter(labs, creat != 0)`
options.feedback:
This removes patient 104 entirely — and with them, their potassium,
which was perfectly good. You only wanted to mark one value as
missing, not lose the whole patient. And because it's stored back into
`labs`, the patient is gone for good.

options.text: `labs$creat == NA`
options.feedback:
This doesn't store anything — it only asks a question. And it's the
question from module 6 that never works: comparing with `NA` gives `NA`
for every value.

options.text: `labs$creat <- NA`
options.feedback:
That replaces the *whole column* with `NA` — one value fills every
row, as in module 9. Every creatinine would be gone.

title: Nobody has high potassium
prompt:
A revised version of the script has:

```r
nrow(labs[labs$K > 5.5, ])
```

```
[1] 0
```

No error, no warning. The report now says no patients have a high
potassium. What happened?
hint: Look at the column name closely, and compare it with the **Data** panel.

options.text: The column is `k`, not `K` — so `$` gave back nothing, and nothing was kept
options.feedback:
Right. `labs$K` doesn't exist, and `$` with a wrong name gives back
`NULL`, silently. A question asked of nothing keeps nothing, so the
count is zero — and it reads like a real result.

A count that's suddenly zero, or much smaller than you expected, is
worth a second look. The check is the same as before: count it by
hand.

options.text: Once the values are numbers, none are over 5.5
options.feedback:
Three of them are, as your count showed. The difference is the capital
`K` — there's no column by that name.

options.text: The 5.5 needs quotes, because `k` is text
options.feedback:
Quotes wouldn't help — the problem comes first. There's no column
called `K` at all. Compare the name with the Data panel.

title: What would have caught them?
prompt:
One more — nothing new, just things you already know coming together.

This case had three problems: a potassium column stored as text, two
impossible creatinines, and a misspelled column name. None of them caused
an error. What would have caught all three?
hint: Think about what you actually did to find each one.

options.text: Looking at the data with `str()` and `summary()`, and checking each result against something you already know
options.feedback:
Right — three habits. Look at how R sees the data (`str()`). Look at
the spread (`summary()`). And check each result against something you
know: a count by hand, a typical value, a second way of getting the
same answer.

None of them needs an error message, which is exactly why they matter
here. When R stops, it tells you. When it doesn't, these are how you
find out.

options.text: Pasting the script into an AI and asking it to find the errors
options.feedback:
An AI reads your code, but these problems aren't in the code. They're
in the data: the word "hemolysed", the 0, the 88. Unless you show it
what the data looks like — which means running `str()` and
`summary()` first — it can't see them. It might spot the capital `K` if
the script uses both spellings, but not the rest.

options.text: Adding `na.rm = TRUE` everywhere
options.feedback:
That would hide problems rather than find them. It quietly leaves out
missing values — it can't tell you a creatinine is in the wrong unit,
or that a column is text.

options.text: Running the script again
options.feedback:
Running it again gives the same wrong answers, just as confidently.
Nothing in the code changes between runs.
